pages.text: Street art in Russia has changed a lot since 2022. Before the war, many artists made art in public spaces. When the war started, some artists left the country. Others stayed but stopped making protest art. Some artists now make large paintings that support the war on big buildings. Some artists were sent to jail for their work.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  04

pages.text: For example, Sasha Skochilenko changed price tags in a store to share anti-war messages. She was in a penal colony for a long time. She was released in 2024 and now lives in another country. Today, it is very dangerous to make protest art in Russia.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  06

pages.text: The government censors the word “war.” Many artists who left Russia now make art about missing their home. Inside Russia, protest art is now very small and anonymous. People use stickers or small drawings to show their feelings. Artist Slava PTRK says that making art in Russia is now almost impossible.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  05

evidence: Through the artists’ narrative, Global Voices traces how street artists in Russia — starting with protests in 2022 — were either pushed out of the country, or prosecuted and sent to jail.
Administrative and criminal cases began, the word “war” was censored , and making direct political statements became increasingly dangerous.
What remains are small acts of protest.

pages.text: The landscape of Russian street art has shifted dramatically since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. According to insights from artist Slava PTRK, the community has fractured: many creators fled into exile, some chose to remain silent, and others began producing state-sanctioned, monumental murals. This evolution marks a departure from the vibrant, independent scene that grew following the 1980s.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  04

pages.text: Repression has become a defining feature of the current environment. Activists like Sasha Skochilenko faced severe consequences for their dissent; she was sentenced to seven years in a penal colony for replacing price tags with anti-war messages before her release in 2024.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  06

pages.text: As the state intensified its control, the word “war” was censored, and public spaces were cleared of direct political statements. While large-scale anti-war art has largely vanished, small-scale resistance persists. Ordinary citizens continue to use stickers and symbolic gestures to express dissent, though these acts are now anonymous.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  05

pages.text: Meanwhile, artists abroad have shifted their focus toward themes of displacement and identity. Slava PTRK notes that while the art scene has not necessarily become stronger, the ability to make any public statement inside Russia has become nearly impossible.

evidence: When the Russian invasion of and subsequent war with Ukraine started in February 2022, street artists, like many people in Russia, were divided.
A few street artists and activists – like Sasha Skochilenko, who was sentenced to seven years in a penal colony for swapping out a store’s price tags with anti-war slogans — were prosecuted.
In the first months after the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, public space in Russia became sites of spontaneous anti-war protest.

pages.text: The trajectory of Russian street art has undergone a profound transformation since the onset of the war in 2022. Historically, the medium emerged during the late Soviet era, flourishing alongside samizdat and underground music. However, the current geopolitical climate has effectively dismantled the independent street art subculture.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  04

pages.text: As documented by Global Voices through the perspective of exiled artist Slava PTRK, the community has been decimated by state-led repression, forcing a diaspora of talent to relocate to countries including Georgia, Germany, and Serbia. The state’s response to dissent has been uncompromising.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  06

pages.text: The case of Sasha Skochilenko, who endured imprisonment for replacing supermarket price tags with anti-war slogans, exemplifies the risks associated with public expression. Following her release in 2024, her story remains a poignant reminder of the dangers inherent in challenging the official narrative.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Anti-war graffiti, Baumana street, Kazan  2022-02-27  05

pages.text: Consequently, the public sphere has been sanitized of anti-war sentiment, with the term “war” itself subject to strict censorship. In its place, the state has promoted monumental, pro-war imagery, utilizing multi-storey murals to project patriotic themes and Soviet-style propaganda. Despite the disappearance of overt political art, a clandestine form of resistance persists.

Anthropologist Alexandra Archipova has cataloged these ephemeral artifacts—stickers, symbolic gestures, and coded inscriptions—that signify a quiet, anonymous defiance. For those in exile, the thematic focus has migrated toward the existential challenges of displacement, loneliness, and the loss of identity.

Ultimately, as Slava PTRK observes, the capacity for meaningful artistic intervention within Russia has been severely curtailed, rendering the prospect of impactful public statements nearly impossible under the current regime.

title: Too young to run, old enough to protest: West Africa’s unfinished democratic bargain
sourceTitle: Too young to run, old enough to protest: West Africa’s unfinished democratic bargain
headline: Too young to run, old enough to protest
author: Adesewa Olofinko
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: In 2018, young people in Nigeria won a big change. The Not Too Young To Run campaign helped lower the age limits for people who want to run for office. However, it is still hard for young people to join politics. It costs a lot of money to apply for these jobs.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 2

pages.text: In some places, the fee is 100 million naira (USD 75,000). This is more money than the job pays in four years. In September 2026, young people met in Dakar, Senegal. They talked about these problems at the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 11

pages.text: Young people are 70 percent of the population in West Africa, but they are not in many decision-making jobs. Political parties control who can run for office. They often choose people with money and power. Leaders at the meeting said this is a contradiction.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 12

pages.text: Young people are old enough to vote and protest, but they are told they need more experience. The goal is to help young people have a real voice in their countries.

evidence: In 2018, young Nigerians won a fight that had taken years to organise.
The Not Too Young To Run campaign helped push through a constitutional amendment lowering the age limits for several elective offices.
Young people make up about 70 percent of the region’s population, according to the conference communiqué .

pages.text: The Not Too Young To Run campaign in Nigeria achieved a significant milestone in 2018 by lowering age limits for elective offices. Despite this legal victory, young aspirants face daunting financial barriers. Nomination fees for political positions can reach 100 million naira (USD 75,000), a sum that often exceeds the total salary of the office itself.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 2

pages.text: Furthermore, recent changes to the Electoral Act 2026 have increased spending limits, making it even harder for young candidates to compete against established politicians. These challenges were central to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference held in Dakar from September 8 to 10, 2026.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 11

pages.text: While young people represent 70 percent of the region's population, they remain largely excluded from formal decision-making. Political parties act as gatekeepers, prioritizing candidates with deep pockets and existing networks. Nelson Asusiya, a Ghanaian parliamentarian, noted that young people are frequently used as symbols for political movements but are rarely granted genuine authority.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 12

pages.text: Civil society leaders like Ezenwa Nwagwu highlight the contradiction of a system that expects youth to vote and protest while denying them office due to a lack of experience. As the region navigates political shifts, including the withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger from ECOWAS, the need for youth inclusion remains a critical, albeit difficult, goal.

evidence: The Not Too Young To Run campaign in Nigeria showed what organised pressure can achieve.
Political parties remain important gatekeepers , controlling who gets nominated, how candidates are selected and, in many cases, whose networks and resources can carry them through an election.

Ezenwa Nwagwu, a Nigerian civil society leader, called the result a contradiction: Young people are old enough to vote and old enough to protest, but are often told they need experience before they can hold political office.

pages.text: The 2018 success of Nigeria’s Not Too Young To Run campaign represented a landmark constitutional shift, yet eight years later, the practical reality for young political aspirants remains bleak. The democratization of candidacy has been undermined by exorbitant financial requirements; nomination forms can cost as much as 100 million naira (USD 75,000).
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 2

pages.text: In one instance, a local government chairmanship fee was set at 30 million naira (USD 22,000), a figure reportedly surpassing the official earnings of the position over a full four-year term. With the enactment of the Electoral Act 2026, which significantly raised campaign spending ceilings, the fiscal barrier to entry has become increasingly insurmountable for the youth demographic.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 11

pages.text: From September 8 to 10, 2026, the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference in Dakar served as a forum to address this systemic exclusion. Although young people constitute 70 percent of the regional population, they remain marginalized within decision-making bodies. Political parties function as entrenched gatekeepers, dictating nominations based on resource access rather than merit.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Protest in Ghana 12

pages.text: Nelson Asusiya, a delegate from Ghana, articulated the frustration of a generation treated as political window dressing while being denied substantive power. The discourse in Dakar also touched upon the broader regional instability, specifically the withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger from ECOWAS. Despite these geopolitical ruptures, the core issues of democratic governance and youth participation persist.

Ezenwa Nwagwu emphasized that the current state of affairs is a fundamental contradiction: young citizens are deemed capable of voting and protesting, yet are dismissed as inexperienced when seeking office. As ECOWAS officials look toward the future, including the proposed West Africa Youth Observer Network, the central challenge remains whether the region can move beyond symbolic inclusion to address the prohibitive costs that effectively bar the youth from the democratic process.
